summary: Noble held several IDIQ supply contracts with the Defense Logistics Agency (the FSG-53, FESE, PACOM MRO, and SOE contracts), most of which had already expired, been non-renewed, or been terminated for cause before Noble's bankruptcy filing, leaving thousands of delivery orders in various states of completion. After the August 30, 2026 petition date, DFAS (DLA's payment processor) placed an administrative hold on roughly $3.2 million (later shown to be about $6.97 million) in payments owed to Noble on prepetition invoices, in order to preserve the government's right to set off debts it says Noble owes it — chiefly a ~$7.9 million net FSG-53 performance disincentive and a ~$2.9-3.5 million False Claims Act settlement balance. Noble filed an emergency motion (Dkt. 102) to compel DLA to pay the held invoices and to enforce the automatic stay; the United States/DLA objected (Dkt. 124), arguing the contracts were not executory, the amounts were not yet due, and a creditor may temporarily withhold payment to protect a setoff right under Citizens Bank of Maryland v. Strumpf. After hearings on September 16 and 18, 2026, and after the parties failed to agree on a form of order (Dkt. 142), the Court ruled (Dkt. 151) that DLA's freeze had gone further than Strumpf allows and ordered DLA to release the improperly withheld funds, net of the undisputed settlement debt, while preserving DLA's right to seek stay relief later to litigate and exercise setoff over the remaining disputed amounts.

timeline.event: Effective date of the FSG-53 Contract (an IDIQ contract encompassing five underlying DLA contract numbers), which included a 1-year transition period and a 3-year base ordering period (Oct. 2023-Sept. 2026) with unexercised option periods.

DLA notifies Noble that it will not exercise the FSG-53 Contract's first option period, effectively ending the ordering period as of September 30, 2026 (though completion of pending orders continues after that).

Noble (successor to Noble Sales Co., Inc.) executes a False Claims Act Settlement Agreement with the United States (DOJ/Dept. of the Air Force) related to a Cannon Air Force Base contract, agreeing to pay $1,034,495.99 plus 5% interest in six semi-annual installments.
FESE Contract ordering period expires after DLA declines to exercise the first option period; 150 delivery orders are later terminated for cause prepetition, 10 remain open.
PACOM MRO Contract and all its option periods expire; 1,217 delivery orders are later terminated for cause prepetition, 132 remain open.

First of three DLA notifications (also Aug. 17 and Sept. 1, 2026) to Noble of its intent to cancel a combined 11,893 outstanding FSG-53 delivery orders (of 20,380 outstanding as of the petition date); Noble did not object to the July/August notices, and the bankruptcy filing stayed DLA from formally modifying the contract to reflect the cancellations.

DLA issues notices of termination for cause on the SOE Contract, terminating it and 2,669 delivery orders; Noble indicated it intended to appeal under the Contract Disputes Act but, per DLA, had not filed a certified claim or appeal by mid-September.

Petition Date. DFAS has an administrative hold in place on payments due to Noble (under CAGE Code 1HEN9) for prepetition goods/services; held invoices total approximately $3,226,144.26 as of DLA's objection.

Debtors file an Emergency Motion (Dkt. 102) for an order compelling DLA to perform/pay under the contracts (~$3,226,144.26), enforcing the automatic stay, and ordering DLA to cease alleged stay violations.

United States, on behalf of DLA, files its Objection (Dkt. 124), arguing the contracts are not executory (IDIQ, expired/terminated), amounts are not yet due under the Prompt Payment Act, and the temporary hold is a lawful preservation of setoff rights under Strumpf given DLA's claims (net FSG-53 disincentive of $7,907,033.24 for Years 1-2, and an accelerated FCA settlement claim of $2,921,275.69 after 3 of 6 installments paid). First hearing held same day; a WAWF snapshot at 1:14 p.m. ET that day shows $6,972,618 owed across 879 invoices.

Unable to agree on a form of order after the hearing, the United States files a Certification of Counsel (Dkt. 142) attaching its own proposed order and a blackline against the Debtors' competing version; the U.S.'s proposed order would have released only $6,972,618 pending a further stay-relief/estimation process, subject to DLA's continued ability to reinstate blocks above a $10,290,636.04 payable threshold.

Second hearing held. The Court finds DLA's administrative freeze exceeded what Strumpf permits (it covered more than was reasonably necessary to protect DLA's setoff rights, and DLA never promptly sought a setoff order); orders DLA to pay Noble $6,972,618 (the amount improperly frozen) minus the $538,183.63 the Debtors acknowledge is owed on the FCA settlement, i.e. $6,434,434.37, within three business days. The Court also denies the United States' request for a stay pending appeal (or an administrative stay), citing Noble's urgent liquidity need to avoid conversion to chapter 7.

outcome: A partial, court-imposed resolution that leaned in Noble's favor on the immediate cash-flow issue but preserved DLA's underlying setoff claims for later litigation. Judge Goldblatt granted the Debtors' emergency motion 'to the extent set forth' in the order: he ruled that DLA's blanket administrative freeze on Noble's payables exceeded what Citizens Bank of Maryland v. Strumpf permits (DLA could have paid amounts coming due without prejudicing its setoff rights, and unlike the creditor in Strumpf, DLA never promptly moved for setoff relief). The Court ordered DLA to pay Noble $6,434,434.37 within three business days — the $6,972,618 in improperly frozen payables, netted against the $538,183.63 Noble concedes it owes under the FCA settlement agreement. Going forward, DLA must pay Noble in the ordinary course and cannot reinstate any freeze or exercise setoff/replacement rights without first obtaining stay relief from the Court; if DLA believes future payables are not adequately protecting its claims (e.g., the disputed ~$7.9 million FSG-53 disincentive claim), it may file a stay-relief motion, and the Court will conduct a Section 502(c) estimation proceeding to size the competing claims. The order was effective immediately, and the Court denied the government's request for a stay pending appeal given Noble's urgent liquidity needs.
financial_stakes: Administrative hold on Noble's prepetition invoices: initially described as ~$3,226,144.26 (per the Debtors' motion and DLA's objection), but the WAWF-verified figure at the time of the September 16 hearing was $6,972,618 across 879 invoices — the amount the Court ultimately found had been improperly frozen. Net amount the Court ordered DLA to actually remit: $6,434,434.37 (after offsetting the undisputed FCA settlement debt). Offsetting claims asserted by DLA/the United States: (1) a net FSG-53 performance disincentive of $7,907,033.24 for Years 1-2 (Year 1 disincentive $8,303,730.26 less Year 2 incentive $396,697.02; Year 3 not yet calculated); (2) an accelerated False Claims Act settlement claim, cited as $2,921,275.69 in DLA's objection but resolved at $538,183.63 (per the Sept. 18 order) / $537,672.89 (per the Sept. 17 competing proposed order) as the amount actually owed and setoff in this ruling, out of an original $3,481,737.91 accelerated-default claim; (3) a DOJ estimate that potential FCA exposure from ~500 investigated transactions on the underlying Cannon Air Force Base contract could exceed $7.8 million if liability and treble damages/penalties applied (not a final claim, and not representative of the full universe of transactions under that contract). Note: no figures resembling a ~$400 million contract termination or an ~$86 million claim appear anywhere in the dockets reviewed (0124, 0142, 0151) — the disincentive, settlement, and administrative-hold amounts above are the only dollar figures the DLA dispute documents disclose.
